title: School Improvement 201: What to Actually Do With Your Summer
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien argues that most summer leadership retreats produce aspiration without implementation, resulting in plans that quietly die by October. The article is a practical framework for principals who have already done the strategic work—set OKRs, named the destination—and now need to translate vision into operational reality before the school year begins. O'Brien structures summer work in three layers: first, aligning leadership teams by translating OKRs into specific systems, behaviors, and dated milestones with clear ownership; second, defining school culture with behavioral precision so that teachers can model and practice the exact routines they will run on Day 1; and third, designing the student experience backward from what a student will feel in the first ninety seconds of the school day. Throughout, he insists that leadership development happens through exposure to ambiguous problems and judgment work, not through decks and OKRs—and that the whole job of summer is to make September 'boring, predictable, designed.' The article is targeted at school leaders but contains transferable principles about the gap between strategy and implementation that apply to any organizational leadership context.
points: The failure mode of summer planning is confusing alignment on vision with alignment on work: teams that agree on 'what' but never decide 'how,' 'who,' and 'by when' will improvise once school starts—and improvisation at scale is chaos with good intentions.

Every system needs a name, not a committee: real ownership means one person is responsible for running it, one person supports it, and the principal knows where to maximize their own involvement versus where to step back and lead leaders.

Culture cannot be communicated by adjectives: defining 'high expectations' requires naming the observable adult behaviors in specific moments (what does the teacher do when a kid puts their head down?), not aspiring to values in a PD session.

The first 18 days install the foundation everything else depends on: leadership teams should not just discuss but rehearse the opening of school in sequence until they can run it without the principal in the room.

Design the student experience backward from the first ninety seconds: a student doesn't experience your OKRs—they experience whether someone knew their name, whether they understood what was expected of them, or had to guess.
quotes: Summer is not for more dreaming. Summer is for translating those OKRs into systems, systems into behaviors, and behaviors into milestones with dates on them. That's the gap between a design and an implementation — and it's where almost every school improvement plan quietly dies.

You agreed on what. You never agreed on how. Or who. Or by when. You set a goal to move proficiency, and never decided which three teacher behaviors actually move it, who's responsible for installing them, and what they should look like by the second week versus the second month.

A plan is not an implementation. An OKR is not a system. And a leadership team that has dreamed together but not built together is a team that will improvise once the building fills up — and improvisation, at scale, across thirty adults and four hundred kids, is just chaos with good intentions.
The whole job of the summer is to make September boring. Predictable. Designed.

Buy-in doesn't come from a poster. It comes from clarity plus competence — from teachers walking in knowing exactly what the culture is, what it looks like when they do it, and feeling ready to deliver it the same way the teacher next door will.

A leadership team should leave the summer able to answer one question instantly, in unison: when this system breaks in October, who handles it and how? If you get blank stares, you have more summer work to do.
